extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and claim drafters (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, case-law–based guidance for drafting and evaluating U.S. patent claims and specifications, focusing on subject-matter eligibility, claim scope/limitations, specification language, means-plus-function treatment, software structure, and multi-actor method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility — natural phenomena (DNA testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to naturally occurring substances (e.g., cell-free fetal DNA) may be ineligible when the existence of the substance is a natural phenomenon and the claimed steps of analyzing that substance are well understood, routine, and conventional; discovery of the natural phenomenon alone is not enough to make related conventional steps patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Ariosa Diagnostics, Inc. v. Sequenom, Inc.: the court found the existence of cffDNA to be a natural phenomenon and the claimed analytic steps routine, concluding that claiming conventional steps based on a discovery about a naturally occurring substance does not make a claim patent-eligible. (See § 1:4, note 34.1.) Consider whether claimed steps add more than the discovery of a natural law or phenomenon; reciting only conventional activity tied to a natural fact risks ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility — software-based inventions (abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software-based patents may be rejected as claiming an abstract idea when the claimed steps describe a process 'devoid of a concrete or tangible application'; merely adding novel or non-routine components to an abstract idea does not necessarily make it patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ultramercial, Inc. v. Hulu, LLC rejected an eleven-step Internet-distribution method as an abstract idea because the steps described an abstract process without a concrete/tangible application and noted that adding novel/non-routine components may not convert an abstraction into something concrete. However, not all software claims will be abstract — DDR Holdings (rare) found eligibility where the patent addressed a problem unique to the Internet and asserted an Internet-based solution. When drafting, identify a concrete technological solution to a technical problem and avoid claiming only abstract business/mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble may be a claim limitation when it provides necessary structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble phrase can function as a claim limitation if it provides necessary structure to the claimed invention; conversely, a preamble stating purpose or function (e.g., 'generating') may be nonlimiting and not provide antecedent basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TomTom, Inc. v. Adolph: the phrase 'a method for generating and updating data for use in a destination tracking system of at least one mobile unit' — the 'destination tracking system' language was treated as a claim limitation providing necessary structure, but the purpose word 'generating' was nonlimiting. Draft preambles carefully and consider whether the preamble supplies structural limitations or merely states purpose; courts will analyze whether preamble language is necessary to give life to claimed elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification language such as 'constitutes a distinctive advantage' does not necessarily limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases in the specification that describe advantages (e.g., 'constitutes a distinctive advantage') do not, by themselves, limit the invention to particular embodiments unless there is a clear disavowal in the prosecution history that the step is optional or excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cadence Pharmaceuticals Inc. v. Exela PharmSci, Inc. held that 'constitutes a distinctive advantage' did not imply limitation to particular embodiments because the prosecution history lacked a clear disavowal of the step. Avoid inadvertently limiting claim scope by using specification language that could be read as disclaiming alternatives; if narrowing is intended, make explicit statements in the prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification — whether to include 'objects of the invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: Including 'objects of the invention' in the specification is common in some jurisdictions but raises substantive questions: are satisfaction of such objects prerequisites for infringement, for determining utility, or for claim definiteness? Are the objects merely introductory guidance, and must they have been accomplished or be possible to accomplish?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author questions the practice and warns drafters to consider potential consequences of listing objects: they may be read by courts or examiners in ways that affect claim interpretation, utility, or definiteness. If including objects, be cautious about their phrasing and avoid implying unnecessary limitations or prerequisites unless intended. (See § 3:10, note 262.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from absence of the term 'means' is rebuttable when claim language fails to recite sufficient structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional 'strong' presumption that absence of the word 'means' avoids means-plus-function treatment can be overcome: if a claim term (including nonce words) fails to define sufficiently definite structure or instead recites a function without sufficient structure, the presumption may be rebutted and means-plus-function interpretation applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lighting World (2004) characterized the presumption as 'strong,' but Williamson v. Citrix Online, LLC (June 2015) changed that, permitting courts to find means-plus-function treatment despite the absence of the word 'means' where structure is lacking. When drafting, express structural details clearly; avoid using purely functional or nonce terms without disclosing corresponding structure in the specification. (See § 3:29.5, note 526.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure required in software claims — disclose at least one algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For software-implemented functions, the 'corresponding structure' under §112 is the algorithm itself; absent disclosure of at least one algorithm, a software claim may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eon Corp. IP Holdings LLC v. AT&T Mobility LLC: the court stated that 'the corresponding structure for a function performed by a software algorithm is the algorithm itself.' To resist indefiniteness and means-plus-function pitfalls, include disclosure of algorithms or sufficient structural detail in the specification, or claim more concrete, tangible implementations. (See § 3:29.8, note 587.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement of multi-step method claims requires attribution of all steps to a single entity
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for direct infringement of a method claim comprising multiple steps requires that all of the method steps be attributable to one entity — either because one entity performs all steps, an entity directs or controls another's performance (agency/contract), or participants form a joint enterprise — but courts must determine in each case whether the accused actions are attributable to a single entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Akamai Technologies, Inc. v. Limelight Networks, Inc. (en banc, Aug. 2015) clarified that direct infringement requires attribution of all steps to one entity, and described direction/control and joint enterprise as ways to satisfy that test. When drafting method claims, consider drafting alternatives (system/apparatus claims, claim steps structured so a single actor performs them, or express steps that minimize risk of divided infringement) and consider relevant contractual/agency relationships that could create attribution. (See § 7:3, note 12.)
